hook.text: Counting words. Guessing the next word from the last one. Giving rare words extra weight. These ideas are much older than they look.

age.text: The youngest of the three is over fifty. The oldest is over ninety.

order.text: So here's how the field got here, oldest first.

zipf.text: It starts in the nineteen thirties, when the linguist George Zipf counted words.

law.text: Rank them by how common they are, and the second word turns up about half as often as the first, the tenth a tenth as often. On these log scales, that's a straight line: Zipf's law.

emma.text: Here's the course's count of Jane Austen's Emma. The top is rough: the first two words almost tie.

tail.text: But a hundred words make up sixty percent of the book, and of its seven thousand different words, nearly four in ten appear just once.

zipf-out.text: Next, counts like these became a way to predict.

shannon.text: In nineteen forty-eight, Claude Shannon founded information theory.

guess.text: Tucked inside his paper: guess the next word from the one before, by how often each word follows another.

book.text: He even made text that way, by hand: open a book at random, find the word, copy the one after it, repeat.

sample.text: Here's what came out. The head and in frontal attack on an English writer... It reads like English, and says nothing.

demo.text: The course's tiny version does the same: after the word the, cat comes three times and dog twice, so it guesses cat.

ngram.text: That's an n-gram model. Today's language models still make that guess, with far more than counts behind it.

shannon-out.text: But could a machine that strings words together ever hold a conversation?

turing.text: In nineteen fifty, Alan Turing asked whether machines can think, then swapped that question for a test.

game.text: A judge trades typed messages with a hidden person and a hidden machine. If the judge can't tell which is which, the machine passes.

name.text: He called it the imitation game. We call it the Turing test, and every chatbot since has been chasing it.

turing-out.text: Four years later, a demo made that goal look close.

georgetown.text: In nineteen fifty-four, Georgetown and IBM showed a computer translating Russian into English.

small.text: It knew two hundred and fifty words and six grammar rules, and translated about sixty hand-picked sentences.

hype.text: The papers loved it. One of its leaders predicted working translation in five years, perhaps three.

alpac.text: Twelve years later, a government committee saw no near-term prospect of useful machine translation, and the funding dried up.

moral.text: A polished demo is not a working system.

georgetown-out.text: And that same year, a tiny program at MIT showed a subtler trap.

eliza.text: Joseph Weizenbaum wrote Eliza, a program that played a therapist.

rules.text: Its whole trick: spot a phrase like I need, and hand it back as a question.

confided.text: There's no understanding in it at all. Yet people confided in it. Weizenbaum's own secretary asked him to leave the room.

effect.text: Seeing real understanding in a simple text trick is now called the Eliza effect.

eliza-out.text: Meanwhile, the quiet counting kept paying off.

sparck.text: In nineteen seventy-two, Karen Spark Jones, at Cambridge, saw a flaw in how search matched words.

flaw.text: A match on a common word counted just as much as a match on a rare one.

fix.text: Her fix: the fewer documents a word appears in, the more a match on it is worth.

example.text: In her example of two hundred documents, a word in ninety weighs two, and a word in just three weighs seven.

idf.text: That's inverse document frequency, the IDF in TF-IDF, and search engines still lean on it today.

sparck-out.text: The last story jumps ahead four decades.

w2v.text: In twenty thirteen, Tomash Mikolov and colleagues at Google released word to vec.

points.text: It gives every word a point in space, and words used in similar places land close together.

analogy.text: And directions mean something. Start at king, take away man, add woman, and the nearest other word is queen.

great.text: Remember great and excellent, two unrelated columns in a bag of words? Here, they're neighbors.

close.text: Put it all on one line, and a thread runs through it: each new idea kept the one beneath it.

layers.text: Word vectors still start from tokens. Search still leans on IDF. Language models still guess the next word.

warnings.text: And two warnings came along: a demo isn't a system, and fluent text isn't understanding.

end.text: So what you learned here isn't a stage the field left behind. It's the ground everything since is built on.
